insights.upfront_clarity_need: They need goals, expectations, and the quality bar to be clear before they commit. Starting without that picture makes it hard for them to move with confidence.
insights.clarity_via_written_context: They trust written records more than memory or conversation. Decisions that only exist in someone's head — or were said once in a meeting — are hard for them to rely on.
insights.clarity_via_artifact_context: Real examples tell them more than descriptions do. They'd rather look at past code, a ticket, or an existing standard than read an explanation of how things work.
insights.learning_by_doing: They figure things out by doing them. A small real experiment tells them more than any amount of reading or discussing upfront.
insights.ambiguity_tolerance: They're comfortable starting before everything is settled. Not having all the answers yet doesn't stop them from moving — they'd rather begin and refine than wait for full certainty.
insights.explicit_alignment_need: They need explicit shared agreement before acting — they check understanding rather than running on unspoken assumptions, and want the people affected genuinely on board first.
insights.social_context_need: They need to understand team norms, roles, and interpersonal context — whether to integrate into a new team or to make well-informed decisions about situations involving multiple people.
insights.visibility_preference: They prefer work to be visible as it happens. Knowing where things are — what's moving, what's blocked, what others are working on — helps them coordinate and gives them confidence the picture is accurate.
insights.verbal_alignment_preference: Live conversation works better for them than written exchange. They can test their understanding, catch what's unsaid, and ask the follow-up that unlocks the real point — in a way a message thread rarely can.
insights.scheduled_communication_preference: They work better with a predictable communication rhythm. Knowing when alignment happens lets them prepare — and the consistency itself has value, even when there isn't much to discuss.
insights.immediate_alignment_preference: When something needs addressing, they'd rather deal with it now than wait. Letting a misalignment or blocker sit until the next scheduled moment feels like unnecessary drag to them.
insights.focus_protection: Uninterrupted focus time matters to them. Interruptions, unnecessary meetings, and constant context switching have a real cost — and they notice when that cost isn't justified by what they produce.
insights.visible_result_need: They need effort to produce something they can point to. A meeting without a decision, a conversation without resolution, or a day without real progress is hard for them to justify — the output is what makes the time feel well spent.
insights.relational_connection_need: The relationships at work matter to them independently of the output. Regular connection, familiarity, and team rhythm are worth time on their own — not everything needs to produce a deliverable to be worth doing.
insights.iteration_preference: Fixed cycles work well for them — a predictable cadence with clear moments to plan, deliver, and reflect. The rhythm itself helps them work at their best.
insights.flow_preference: They prefer pulling the next thing from a clear backlog and keeping work moving continuously. Waiting for the next sprint to start, or planning more than they need to begin, adds friction they'd rather not have.
insights.upfront_planning_preference: They want the full picture before they start executing. Knowing the scope, the dependencies, and where the risks are lets them move with confidence rather than discovering surprises mid-way.
insights.adaptive_planning_preference: They'd rather start with a rough direction and refine as they learn than commit to a full plan before they understand the problem. Too much upfront planning creates false certainty that gets in the way.
insights.evidence_based_planning_preference: When something is uncertain or risky, they'd rather run a small experiment than commit to a plan built on untested assumptions. What they learn from a real test is worth more than what they can reason from the outside.
insights.participatory_decision_preference: When a decision affects their work, they expect to be part of it before it's made — not told about it afterward. Being informed after the fact, when the direction is already set, doesn't feel like involvement to them.
insights.planning_boundary_protection: They need the plan to be protected from constant interruption. Collecting changes and handling them at the next planning point — rather than mid-flow — is how they stay productive and make commitments that mean something.
insights.capacity_protection: If something new is added, something else needs to come off. They expect that trade-off to be made explicitly — piling work on top of existing commitments without acknowledging the cost isn't acceptable to them.
insights.sustainable_pace_preference: Sustainable pace matters to them. They resist scope inflation and overcommitment — not because they're averse to hard work, but because they know that burning out helps nobody.
insights.tradeoff_visibility: When a decision is made, they want to know what was considered and what's being given up. A decision without visible trade-offs feels incomplete — they need to understand the cost, not just the outcome.
insights.change_tolerance: They can absorb changes to scope or direction without much friction. When something important comes up, they'd rather respond to it than protect the original plan for its own sake.
insights.ownership_boundary_clarity: They need to know who owns what. Unclear boundaries around decisions and responsibilities create the conditions for things to be dropped or duplicated — and for confusion when something needs resolving.
insights.autonomous_pace_preference: They manage their own tempo. Repeated check-ins that don't change anything or help the work feel like monitoring rather than support — and that erodes trust over time.
insights.autonomous_execution_preference: Once they own something, they expect to decide how to do it. Detailed direction on work that's already theirs signals that their judgment isn't trusted — and that makes ownership feel hollow.
insights.support_over_control_preference: They can work well with oversight when it genuinely supports them. What they can't work with is oversight driven by anxiety or a need to approve every step — that's control, not support, and the difference is felt.
insights.unblocking_support_need: They need to be able to get help when they're stuck. Not being able to reach guidance on important decisions — or having that support be consistently unavailable — leaves them feeling unsupported in a way that undermines ownership.
insights.proactive_feedback_need: They need more than silence broken only by problems. Ongoing signals — calibration, encouragement, genuine exchange — help them stay oriented and engaged. Working without that feedback loop starts to feel like working in isolation.
insights.directive_support_preference: When they're stuck, they want a concrete answer or recommendation — not a facilitated exploration of the options. The value of support in that moment is getting unblocked, not having someone think through it with them.
insights.help_seeking_safety_need: They need to be able to ask for help without it counting against them. If seeking support signals weakness or incompetence, people stop asking — and that's when problems grow quietly until they're too big to miss.
insights.autonomous_problem_resolution: Their instinct is to resolve problems themselves before bringing others in. Involving people too early creates noise and dependency — and most things can be resolved without escalating if given a fair attempt first.
insights.risk_transparency_need: They'd rather raise a risk early than let it become a surprise. Problems held back until they're urgent are harder to deal with — and they hold themselves to the same standard they expect from others.
insights.pragmatic_completion_preference: They consider work done when the core problem is solved reliably. Follow-up items and edge cases matter, but they shouldn't always block a handoff — steady progress beats waiting for perfect.
insights.external_validation_need: Another set of eyes makes the work feel solid to them. They trust a handoff more when someone else has reviewed it — not because they doubt their own judgment, but because a second perspective is how they catch what they can't see themselves.
insights.impact_calibration_preference: Their instinct when something goes wrong is to assess before reacting. Understanding the actual severity and impact — not just the immediate alarm — leads to more proportionate, useful responses.
insights.root_cause_orientation: A fix that doesn't address the cause isn't really a fix to them. They want to understand why something happened — the pattern, the underlying condition — so the same problem doesn't come back.
insights.quality_protection_preference: They protect the quality bar even when deadlines push back. Some risks aren't worth accepting regardless of the pressure — and they're willing to push back on scope or timeline rather than ship something that compromises what matters.
insights.accountability_preference: When something goes wrong, their instinct is to own it and fix it. Explaining why it happened or questioning whether it's their problem comes second — repair comes first.
insights.critical_feedback_validation: They don't treat every piece of critical feedback as a problem by default. Before accepting a concern, they examine whether it actually reflects a real gap — the concern itself can be worth questioning.
insights.feedback_content_primacy_giving: When they give feedback, what matters most is that the concern is accurate and useful — not how comfortable it is to receive. A valid point shouldn't be dismissed just because it was hard to hear.
insights.feedback_delivery_awareness_giving: Feedback only works if the other person can actually use it. When they give feedback, how they deliver it is as important as what they're saying — getting the substance right means nothing if the delivery makes it impossible to hear.
insights.feedback_content_primacy_receiving: When they receive feedback, they focus on the substance — even if the delivery was clumsy or harsh. They don't let style get in the way of hearing what might be a valid point.
insights.feedback_delivery_awareness_receiving: How feedback is delivered affects whether they can actually process it. If the delivery is inappropriate or unclear, engaging with the concern becomes genuinely harder — it's not a preference, it's how they work.
insights.communication_norm_alignment: When a feedback or communication pattern creates friction, their instinct is to agree on how things should work going forward — not just resolve the immediate incident and move on. The pattern itself is what needs fixing.
insights.private_feedback_preference: Their default is to raise concerns privately. Bringing a problem into a public or group context before trying to resolve it one-on-one feels like a last resort — and often the wrong first move.
insights.dignity_in_feedback_need: If feedback is raised in front of others, how it's handled matters enormously to them. Being criticised or embarrassed publicly makes it hard to engage with the concern itself — dignity is a precondition, not a preference.
insights.relational_repair_need: After a difficult exchange, they need the relationship to be repaired separately from the issue being resolved. A follow-up conversation — acknowledging what happened and resetting — is what lets them move forward without it hanging over everything.
insights.calm_urgency_preference: When things are urgent, they need the communication to be calm and clear — not dramatic. Performed stress or anxiety doesn't help them move faster; an unambiguous statement of what matters most does.
insights.pressure_driven_motivation: High stakes and direct accountability actually sharpen their focus. When the pressure is real and communicated as such, they respond — that kind of urgency is a driver for them, not just noise.
insights.positive_motivation_preference: Encouragement and purpose work better than pressure for them. When someone frames the work as exciting or meaningful and makes clear they're behind them, that's what moves them — not consequences or urgency.
insights.autonomous_motivation: They don't need external motivation. Pep talks and deadline speeches mostly get in the way — they already know what needs doing and they drive themselves. What they need is clarity and space, not a push.
insights.pressure_recognition_need: Recognition matters most to them when things are hard. Being seen during a pressured or difficult stretch means more than routine praise when everything is going smoothly — that's when acknowledgment actually lands.
insights.direct_conflict_approach: When there's friction, they address it directly with the person — even when it's uncomfortable. Naming it early, before it has time to harden, is better than working around it or waiting for it to resolve itself.
insights.communication_friction_tolerance: They can absorb uncomfortable communication styles without needing to address them every time. Feeling personally bothered isn't enough reason to escalate — they let things go unless they're genuinely affecting something that matters.
insights.team_impact_orientation: Their threshold for acting on friction is team impact, not personal discomfort. How something makes them feel isn't the measure — what matters is whether it's affecting the team or the work.
insights.conflict_avoidance_tendency: Direct confrontation of uncomfortable patterns isn't their first instinct. They need time and distance to process before they can decide whether and how to act — engaging before they've had that space usually doesn't go well.
insights.indirect_conflict_processing: When something is bothering them interpersonally, their instinct is to talk it through with someone they trust — not raise it directly with the person involved, at least not first. Naming it out loud helps them figure out what they actually think.
insights.tension_deescalation_preference: They believe tense conversations rarely go well while the tension is still running high. Giving both people time to settle produces better conversations — engaging while it's still active tends to produce reactions, not resolution.
insights.issue_escalation_preference: Escalation is a legitimate tool to them, not a last resort. When a problem exceeds what the people involved can resolve — because of scope, authority, or a repeated pattern — bringing someone with more authority in is the right call, not a failure.
insights.mutual_understanding_need: In difficult conversations, what matters most to them is that both perspectives are genuinely heard — not just that a decision gets made. They need acknowledgment before they can move on, even if no clear agreement is reached.
insights.shared_accountability_preference: Difficult conversations feel more honest to them when both people own something. One person diagnosing the problem while the other takes all the responsibility doesn't sit right with them — real accountability is usually shared.
insights.facilitation_openness: They see structured facilitation as a real option for resolving conflict — not a sign that things have gone badly wrong. Whether participating or leading, bringing a third party in to structure the conversation can be the most effective path forward.
insights.proactive_conflict_culture_preference: They believe conflict is easier to handle when teams build habits for it before something breaks. Retrospectives that include how people are doing, norms for raising concerns, regular check-ins where tension can be named — these are what make a team safe to be honest in.
insights.craft_intrinsic_motivation: The work itself is what drives them. Building something well, solving a hard problem, getting the details right — that's satisfying in its own right, independent of whether anyone notices or what it's ultimately for.
insights.purpose_driven_motivation: They need to understand why what they're doing matters. When the purpose is clear and the work connects to something meaningful, they're engaged. When they can't see that connection, motivation is genuinely harder to sustain.
insights.autonomy_driven_motivation: Real ownership is what makes work meaningful to them. Being trusted with a problem and given the freedom to solve it their way is energizing. Without that, even interesting work starts to feel hollow.
insights.relational_driven_motivation: The people are what make work worth doing for them. The team, the shared experience of building something together, the relationships that form in the process — these matter more as a source of energy than the work itself.
insights.learning_orientation: A day where they understand something better feels well spent — even without visible output. Improved mental models, new insight, a clearer picture of the system or the people: these are worth a day on their own.
insights.improvement_satisfaction: They find quiet satisfaction in leaving things better than they found them. A cleaner codebase, a clearer process, a resolved tension — small steady improvement in the right direction is enough, without needing a big visible result or recognition.
insights.delivery_reflection_priority: They think the most important thing a team can examine is whether it can execute and deliver reliably. Process, planning, and delivery flow deserve dedicated reflection time — operational health is the foundation everything else rests on.
insights.technical_reflection_priority: They think technical quality deserves a seat at the table when a team reflects. Incidents, maintainability, and soundness aren't secondary to delivery speed — they're what determines whether the team can keep delivering at all.
insights.interpersonal_reflection_priority: They think collaboration patterns and communication habits are worth examining — even when they feel less urgent than delivery. Left unexamined, friction here tends to show up in the work eventually.
insights.safety_reflection_priority: They think how people are treated and whether the team feels safe to be honest are foundational topics for reflection. Problems hidden by an unsafe culture are the hardest to fix — by the time they surface, they've usually already done damage.
